quests.instruction:
Which idiom fits this workplace scenario?
"Two weeks into the finance role, she was reviewing spreadsheets she didn't understand at all."
quests.hint: It's about being in a situation that requires more skill or experience than you currently have.
quests.explanation: 'Out of your depth' means facing a task beyond your current ability or knowledge. "He felt completely out of your depth leading his first client call."
quests.origin: A swimming metaphor: standing in water deeper than you can safely stand in, with no solid ground beneath your feet.

quests.instruction: Manager: 'Don't worry if the new system feels confusing right now.' New hire: 'Yeah, I expected a bit of a ___.'
quests.hint: It describes how much effort it takes to become competent at something new.
quests.explanation: 'A learning curve' describes the process, often difficult at first, of gaining a new skill. "There's a steep learning curve with this software, but it gets easier."
quests.origin: Originally a graphing term from psychology, plotting how performance improves with practice over time.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "After a rocky first month in the new city, she was finally starting to feel settled and confident."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Become comfortable and confident in a new situation, after an adjustment period.
quests.explanation: 'Find your feet' means to become confident and settled after starting something new. "It took him a semester to find his feet at university."
quests.origin: A literal image of a young animal wobbling before it learns to stand and walk steadily.

quests.word: READ THE WRITING ON THE WALL
quests.instruction: Colleague: 'The department has missed every quarterly target this year.' You: 'Yeah, I think we all need to ___.'
quests.hint: It's about recognizing clear signs that something bad is coming, not literal graffiti.
options: READ THE WRITING ON THE WALL
quests.explanation: 'Read the writing on the wall' means to recognize clear signs that something (often bad) is about to happen. "When two competitors folded, we read the writing on the wall and changed our strategy early."
quests.correctAnswer: READ THE WRITING ON THE WALL
quests.origin: From a biblical story (Daniel 5) in which mysterious handwriting appears on a wall, warning of a king's downfall.

quests.instruction: The city approved the new bike lane a year ago, but construction still hasn't started — officials keep ___.
quests.hint: It means deliberately delaying or being slow to act on something.
quests.explanation: 'Drag your feet' means to act deliberately slowly, often to avoid or delay something. "The insurance company kept dragging its feet on the claim."
quests.origin: A literal image of someone walking reluctantly, feet barely lifting off the ground, extended to reluctant or delayed action.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "The new manager got zero training and was simply left to figure out the job on her own, succeed or fail."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Be left to either succeed through your own effort or fail completely, with no help given.
options: READ THE WRITING ON THE WALL
quests.explanation: 'Sink or swim' describes a situation where someone must succeed on their own, with no support if they struggle. "They threw him into the project with no guidance — total sink or swim."
quests.origin: A literal image from swimming: without help, a person in water either manages to swim or doesn't — there's no in-between.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "She just moved cities and started a new job in the same week — maybe don't be so hard on her about the late report."
quests.hint: It means being more lenient or forgiving toward someone, given their circumstances.
quests.explanation: 'Cut someone some slack' means to be less critical of someone, especially given a valid reason. "He's had a rough month — let's cut him some slack on the deadline."
quests.origin: From sailing, where 'slack' in a rope means extra loose length — giving someone slack means easing the tension instead of pulling tight.

quests.instruction: When two teammates called in sick, the rest of the team had to ___ and cover their tasks.
quests.hint: It means taking on extra work to make up for what someone else isn't doing.
options: READ THE WRITING ON THE WALL
quests.explanation: 'Pick up the slack' means to take on additional responsibility that others aren't handling. "With one designer out, everyone else picked up the slack."
quests.origin: Also from the rope image: 'slack' left hanging needs to be gathered up, or 'picked up,' for the rope to do its job properly.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A fair exchange in which both sides make some compromises.
quests.explanation: 'Give and take' describes a relationship or negotiation where both sides compromise. "A good partnership needs a bit of give and take."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent phrase pairing two opposite verbs to describe mutual compromise, used in English since at least the 1700s.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "I don't mind covering extra shifts, but I refuse to work unpaid overtime every weekend — that's where I stop agreeing."
quests.hint: It's about setting a firm limit on what you're willing to accept or do.
quests.explanation: 'Draw the line' means to set a clear limit on acceptable behavior. "I'll help with extra tasks, but I draw the line at working weekends for free."
quests.origin: From literal boundary lines marking where one area or category ends and another begins.

quests.instruction: When the coach started criticizing players' personal lives, most people felt he had ___.
quests.hint: It means to go beyond acceptable behavior, crossing a limit that shouldn't be crossed.
quests.explanation: 'Overstep the mark' means to go too far, exceeding what is acceptable. "His joke about her accent overstepped the mark."
quests.origin: From a literal 'mark' or boundary line — stepping past it, physically or figuratively, means going beyond what's allowed.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "His comment about her weight during the meeting went from playful teasing to something clearly hurtful and inappropriate."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Do or say something that goes beyond what is acceptable, often violating a boundary.
quests.explanation: 'Cross the line' means to do something that goes past acceptable behavior. "The joke crossed the line, and the room went silent."
quests.origin: Related to 'draw the line' and 'overstep the mark' — a family of idioms all built on the image of a boundary that shouldn't be passed.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "I actually think your plan is solid, but let me push back on a few points just to make sure it holds up."
quests.hint: One idiom means arguing a side you don't necessarily believe, to test it; a different idiom means refusing to pick a side at all — here, the speaker already has an opinion.
quests.explanation: 'Play devil's advocate' fits because the speaker already agrees but is deliberately arguing the other side to stress-test the idea — unlike 'sit on the fence,' which means avoiding forming any opinion at all. "I'll play devil's advocate: what if the client says no?"
quests.origin: From a historical Catholic Church role, the 'advocatus diaboli,' tasked with arguing against a candidate's sainthood to test the case's strength.

quests.instruction: Everyone else on the committee voted clearly for or against the merger, but he refused to say either way — a total ___.
quests.hint: It describes a person, not an action — someone who avoids choosing a side.
quests.explanation: 'A fence-sitter' is someone who consistently avoids taking a clear position. "The other candidates gave real answers, but he stayed a fence-sitter on every issue."
quests.origin: A direct noun form of 'sit on the fence,' describing the person rather than the action.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "He brought up an old argument between two coworkers right before the meeting, clearly hoping to cause conflict."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Deliberately cause trouble or conflict, often by provoking an argument.
quests.explanation: 'Stir the pot' means to deliberately provoke conflict or drama. "She loves stirring the pot by bringing up old grudges at family dinners."
quests.origin: A literal cooking image of stirring a pot to keep its contents moving and active, applied figuratively to keeping conflict active.

quests.word: PUT YOUR FOOT IN YOUR MOUTH
quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "He asked her when the baby was due — she wasn't pregnant."
quests.hint: It means saying something embarrassing or tactless, usually by accident.
options: PUT YOUR FOOT IN YOUR MOUTH
quests.explanation: 'Put your foot in your mouth' means to say something embarrassing or awkward without meaning to. "I really put my foot in my mouth when I asked about her 'husband' — they'd just divorced."
quests.correctAnswer: PUT YOUR FOOT IN YOUR MOUTH
quests.origin: A vivid, almost absurd physical image used since the early 1900s to capture the awkwardness of an accidental verbal blunder.

quests.instruction: In a team where everyone usually stays quiet in meetings, she's known for being willing to ___ even when it's unpopular.
quests.hint: It means expressing your honest opinion, even if others might disagree.
options: PUT YOUR FOOT IN YOUR MOUTH
quests.explanation: 'Speak your mind' means to state your honest opinion openly. "I respect that he speaks his mind, even in tense meetings."
quests.origin: A transparent, long-standing phrase treating opinions as thoughts that can be voiced directly, in use since at least the 1500s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "She wanted to correct her boss's mistake in front of the whole client team, but she held back and said nothing."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Stop yourself from saying something, usually to avoid conflict or embarrassment.
options: PUT YOUR FOOT IN YOUR MOUTH
quests.explanation: 'Bite your tongue' means to deliberately hold back from saying something. "I bit my tongue during the meeting, even though I disagreed with the whole plan."
quests.origin: A literal, almost painful image of physically restraining speech, in figurative use in English since Shakespeare's time.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "Instead of arguing back when her coworker took credit for her idea, she stayed calm and simply corrected the record politely."
quests.hint: It's about handling a conflict with dignity instead of matching the other person's bad behavior.
quests.explanation: 'Take the high road' means to act with integrity and restraint, even when provoked. "He took the high road and didn't respond to the insult publicly."
quests.origin: Contrasts a 'high,' honorable path with a 'low' one — a moral metaphor using elevation to represent virtue, common in English since the 1800s.

quests.instruction: Even though her rival kept posting insults online, she refused to ___ and reply with insults of her own.
quests.hint: It means lowering your standards of behavior to match someone acting badly.
quests.explanation: 'Stoop to someone's level' means to lower your standards to match bad behavior. "I won't stoop to his level and start name-calling."
quests.origin: Uses 'stoop,' meaning to physically bend down, as a metaphor for lowering one's moral standard.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Decide to forget past conflicts and move forward without resentment.
quests.explanation: 'Let bygones be bygones' means to forgive and forget a past disagreement. "After years of not speaking, the sisters agreed to let bygones be bygones."
quests.origin: 'Bygones' simply means things that are past or gone — the phrase has been recorded in English since at least the 1500s.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "After ten years of not speaking, the two former business partners finally agreed to meet for coffee and put the whole conflict behind them."
quests.hint: It's specifically about formally ending a conflict, not just staying quiet about it.
quests.explanation: 'Bury the hatchet' means to make peace and end a conflict. "The two companies buried the hatchet and agreed to collaborate again."
quests.origin: From an Indigenous North American peacemaking custom described in early colonial accounts, in which a hatchet was buried to symbolize an end to fighting.

quests.instruction: Even after he apologized twice, she still refused to speak to him — she really knows how to ___.
quests.hint: It means continuing to feel resentment toward someone long after the original conflict.
quests.explanation: 'Hold a grudge' means to continue resenting someone for something they did in the past. "I don't hold a grudge, but I do remember who showed up for me."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent metaphor treating resentment as something a person can literally grip and refuse to let go of.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "The two coworkers finally sat down and openly discussed the tension between them so they could move forward without awkwardness."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Openly discuss a disagreement or tension so misunderstandings are resolved.
quests.explanation: 'Clear the air' means to resolve tension by talking openly about a problem. "We need to clear the air before this project moves forward."
quests.origin: A literal image of clearing away smoke, dust, or fog so a room becomes visible and breathable again — applied to interpersonal tension.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "He kept bringing up the same rejected proposal for the fifth meeting in a row, even though everyone had already agreed to move on."
quests.hint: It's about continuing to argue a point that's already been settled, uselessly.
quests.explanation: 'Beat a dead horse' means to keep pursuing an issue that's already been resolved or is clearly futile. "We voted on this already — let's not beat a dead horse."
quests.origin: A literal, blunt image: continuing to whip a horse that's already dead achieves nothing, in figurative use since the mid-1800s.

quests.instruction: Their old rivalry has finally cooled down, so maybe it's best if we just ___ instead of bringing it up again.
quests.hint: It means deliberately avoiding a topic to prevent reawakening an old problem.
quests.explanation: 'Let sleeping dogs lie' means to avoid stirring up an old, settled problem. "The dispute is over — let's let sleeping dogs lie."
quests.origin: A literal warning about not disturbing a sleeping dog, which might react badly if woken suddenly, recorded in English since at least the 1300s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A close British-English variant meaning to keep pursuing something that's already hopeless or settled.
quests.explanation: 'Flog a dead horse' is the British-English equivalent of 'beat a dead horse,' meaning to keep pursuing an issue that's already settled or hopeless. "He's still flogging a dead horse about the seating chart from last year's wedding."
quests.origin: The older British form of the same image, using 'flog' (to whip) rather than 'beat' — both describe the same pointless action.

quests.word: MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL
quests.instruction: Which idiom fits: "She sent one email with a typo, and he's been treating it like a career-ending disaster ever since."
quests.hint: It's about exaggerating a small problem into something much bigger than it really is.
options: MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL
quests.explanation: 'Make a mountain out of a molehill' means to blow a minor issue far out of proportion. "It's one late reply — you're making a mountain out of a molehill."
quests.correctAnswer: MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL
quests.origin: A vivid size contrast between a towering mountain and a tiny molehill, recorded in English since at least the 1500s.

quests.instruction: Employee: 'I'm so sorry I mixed up the meeting rooms.' Manager: 'Honestly, it's ___ — we just moved down the hall.'
quests.hint: It's a casual way to say something isn't serious or worth worrying about.
options: A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL
quests.explanation: 'Not a big deal' means something is minor and not worth stressing over. "Don't worry about the typo — it's not a big deal."
quests.origin: A straightforward, modern colloquial phrase using 'deal' in the informal sense of a significant matter.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches this situation: "The auditors found one accounting error, but they suspected it was only a small sign of much bigger problems hidden in the company's books."
quests.hint: DEFINITION: A small, visible part of a much larger problem that is mostly hidden.
options: MAKE A MOUNTAIN OUT OF A MOLEHILL
quests.explanation: 'The tip of the iceberg' means a small visible sign of a much bigger, mostly hidden issue. "The complaint we received is probably just the tip of the iceberg."
quests.origin: From real icebergs, where only about a tenth of the mass shows above the waterline — the rest lies unseen below.
